passage:
At the career fair in their Pune college, Payal from the placement office watched a student named Zubin at the glossy stall. The man there had an easy laugh and the same football jersey Zubin was wearing. "Guaranteed paid internship," he said. "Just a small registration fee today." Zubin grinned and reached for his wallet.
Payal's stomach tightened. None of the stalls charged fees. She hovered, then mumbled, "Um... no stall here takes fees." Zubin half-laughed and glanced past her, still smiling at the jersey man. She knew that look: the fun one gets believed, the awkward one doesn't.
Then Zubin stopped, frowned, and checked the college's official placement list on his phone. No such company. When he looked up, the stall was already packing. He came over to Payal. "Thank you. I nearly didn't listen."

qa.q: What did the man at the stall ask Zubin to pay?
qa.a: A small registration fee today.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling as Zubin reached for his wallet?
qa.a: Payal felt uneasy, her stomach tightening, because she knew no stall charged fees and could see Zubin trusting the friendly man over her.

qa.q: What protective step helped Zubin?
qa.a: He stopped and checked the college's official placement list before paying, instead of going on how friendly the man seemed.

qa.q: How might Zubin see Payal differently after checking the list?
qa.a: He may realise he nearly brushed her off for seeming awkward, and now sees her as the one who was right.

grounding: A placement staff member watches a young man trust a charming, familiar-seeming stranger over her awkward warning, until he checks the facts before paying.

passage:
"The first guy was great," Pradeep said, dropping onto the sofa. "Same college as me, loves cricket, so easy to talk to."
"And the second?" Bhavna asked.
"Bit awkward. Didn't laugh at my jokes. Kept checking his notes."
"Did the first one give references?"
"He said he'd send them later. Why?"
"Because the second one brought his last landlord's number, a salary slip and his ID. The first one wants us to skip the agreement because 'we're all friends here'."
Pradeep paused. "Huh. I just... liked him."
"That's the point. Liking someone isn't the same as being able to trust them. People who want to trick you often make themselves very easy to like."
"Okay. Let's call both references tomorrow."

qa.q: What did the second applicant bring?
qa.a: His last landlord's number, a salary slip and his ID.

qa.q: What might Bhavna be worried about as Pradeep praises the first applicant?
qa.a: Bhavna seems uneasy that Pradeep is being charmed: the likeable one gave no references and wants to skip the agreement, while the awkward one brought proof.

qa.q: What step do they agree on, and why is it wise?
qa.a: They agree to call both references tomorrow, checking facts instead of relying on who seemed likeable.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see the first applicant after Bhavna's point?
qa.a: Pradeep pauses and sees that he had only liked the first applicant, not checked him, so he agrees to call both references.

grounding: Two young people choosing a tenant see how easily they trust the charming, similar applicant and doubt the awkward one.

passage:
I'm Rafiq, and in my second year I learned something unpleasant about myself.
Our flat had three of us. Gurpreet was funny, confident, from my own town, great at cricket. Naresh was the quiet one who stammered and ate alone in his room.
When my phone charger and some cash went missing from my desk, Gurpreet shook his head sadly. "Bro, I saw Naresh in your room yesterday." I believed him instantly. Naresh went pale and tried to explain, but the words came out broken, and I didn't wait for them.
A week later, the building guard showed me the corridor camera. Gurpreet had gone into my room while I was at lectures. Naresh had only knocked to return my plate.
I still think about how quickly I trusted the charming one, the one like me, and how easily I doubted the awkward one. Charm told me nothing. I just liked it.

qa.q: Who did the corridor camera show going into the room?
qa.a: Gurpreet had gone into the room while Rafiq was at lectures.

qa.q: How does Rafiq feel looking back at how quickly he believed Gurpreet?
qa.a: Rafiq feels ashamed and uncomfortable, realising he trusted charm and similarity instead of evidence.

qa.q: What could Rafiq do differently next time?
qa.a: Rafiq could hear both people out, check facts like the camera before deciding, and apologise to Naresh.

qa.q: What was it like for Naresh when Rafiq didn't wait for his explanation?
qa.a: Naresh felt hurt and unheard, going pale as his stammer made it harder to defend himself.

grounding: It shows a young adult trusting a charming flatmate from the same town and doubting an awkward one, until evidence shows the charm meant nothing.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, girls' block, Thursday.
A man visited the common room this week claiming to recruit students for a "paid overseas internship." He was polished, funny, well dressed, and he complimented everyone. The girls loved him. Jyoti, especially, sat in the front row laughing at his jokes.
Parveen, who is shy and speaks haltingly, asked him twice for the company's registration number. The others groaned. Jyoti said loudly, "Why are you so suspicious of everyone?" Parveen went quiet.
I checked the company name myself that evening. There was no such registered firm. I informed the college office and the police helpline and put a notice on the board.
Next morning, Jyoti came to my office, embarrassed. "I liked him because he was nice to us. And I thought Parveen was just being awkward." She has since apologised to Parveen. Both of them are now helping me with a talk on job scams for the juniors.

qa.q: What did Parveen ask the visitor for, twice?
qa.a: Parveen asked him twice for the company's registration number.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel when she came to the warden's office?
qa.a: Jyoti felt embarrassed, realising she trusted the charming visitor and dismissed Parveen only because Parveen seemed awkward.

qa.q: What protective steps did the warden take?
qa.a: The warden checked the company, informed the college office and the police helpline, and put a notice on the board.

qa.q: What was it like for Parveen when the others groaned?
qa.a: Parveen felt dismissed and embarrassed, going quiet even though that question was exactly the right one.

grounding: A warden records a young adult trusting a charming recruiter and doubting an awkward classmate's questions, until checking shows the recruiter was fake.

passage:
Wednesday
Second week of my HR internship. Today I sat in on interviews with Abhinav, the hiring manager.
The first candidate was amazing. Confident, from Lucknow like me, same college, even laughed at the same jokes. I wrote "excellent" before he'd finished his first answer.
The second one stammered, dropped her file, and kept saying "sorry." I wrote "weak communication."
After they left, Abhinav asked me why. I said the first one just felt honest. He didn't say anything, just called the previous employers of both.
The first candidate had never worked at the company on his CV. The second one's old manager said she was the best analyst they'd ever had.
I sat in the washroom for ten minutes feeling sick. I trusted him because he felt like me. I doubted her because she was nervous. Abhinav said, "Everyone does it. That's why we check." I'm Trisha, and I'm going to remember this.

qa.q: What did Abhinav do after the candidates left?
qa.a: He called the previous employers of both.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel after the reference calls?
qa.a: Trisha felt sick and ashamed, seeing that Trisha had trusted the charming, similar candidate and doubted the nervous one without reason.

qa.q: What does Abhinav's approach teach about judging honesty?
qa.a: It shows that checking facts, like references, is more reliable than trusting warmth or confidence.

qa.q: How might the second candidate have felt during the interview?
qa.a: She probably felt anxious and flustered, dropping her file and apologising, unaware that her nervousness said nothing about her skill.

grounding: An intern's diary shows trusting a charming candidate with a shared background and doubting a nervous one, until reference checks reveal the bias.

passage:
Ganga: did you sign up for Kunal's "startup internship" thing?
Rashmi: almost! he's so sweet, remembered my name after one chat, same hometown even
Ganga: same, I liked him instantly
Ganga: but Deb from our lab says the company has no address anywhere online
Rashmi: Deb who never looks up from his laptop? he's just weird
Ganga: that's what I thought too. then it hit me, I believe Kunal because he's fun and I brushed off Deb because he's awkward
Ganga: neither of those is actual evidence
Rashmi: hmm. Kunal did say "don't tell too many people, limited seats"
Ganga: that's the bit that bothered me. and Deb showed me the placement cell never listed it
Rashmi: ok that's uncomfortable 🤔
Ganga: let's ask the placement office tomorrow before we send our ID copies to anyone
Rashmi: fine. and maybe say sorry to Deb for calling him weird

qa.q: What did Deb say about the company?
qa.a: Deb said the company has no address anywhere online, and showed Ganga that the placement cell never listed it.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel on noticing why Kunal seemed believable?
qa.a: Ganga felt uneasy and a little embarrassed, seeing that Kunal was believed because he was fun and Deb was brushed off because he was awkward, and neither was evidence.

qa.q: What protective step do Ganga and Rashmi choose?
qa.a: They decide to ask the placement office before sending ID copies to anyone, which checks the offer through an official channel instead of through Kunal's charm.

qa.q: How might Deb feel about being called weird after trying to warn them?
qa.a: Deb checked real facts to help, so being dismissed as weird could feel hurtful and might make Deb less willing to warn people next time.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult noticing that a charming, similar person was trusted and an awkward one doubted, when warmth was no test of honesty and secrecy was a warning.
